reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) antibodies define a multifocal paraneoplastic syndrome that can affect any level of the nervous system simultaneously
Manifestations include limbic and brainstem encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration, sensory neuronopathy, autonomic failure, and myelitis, often in combination
A painful subacute sensory neuronopathy with loss of proprioception and sensory ataxia is a particularly characteristic feature
Overwhelmingly associated with small-cell lung cancer, which is often occult at presentation
The neurological syndrome usually precedes the cancer diagnosis and should trigger an intensive tumour search
Because the target antigens are intracellular and damage is T-cell mediated, neurological recovery is often limited even with treatment
Management combines treatment of the underlying tumour with immunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Anti-Hu encephalomyelitis is driven by an immune response against Hu antigens, RNA-binding proteins expressed by small-cell lung cancer and also by neurons throughout the central and peripheral nervous system. The cross-reactive immune attack, believed to be predominantly cytotoxic T-cell mediated against these intracellular antigens, produces inflammation and neuronal loss at multiple sites, giving the characteristic multifocal picture. The dorsal root ganglia are frequently targeted, producing sensory neuronopathy, while limbic, brainstem, cerebellar, autonomic, and spinal involvement reflect the widespread neuronal expression of the antigen. The intracellular location of the target and the resulting neuronal destruction account for the generally poor neurological response to immunotherapy.
additionalDifferentials: Other autoimmune limbic encephalitides (e.g. anti-NMDA-receptor, LGI1)
Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration from other antibodies
Sensory neuronopathy from Sjogren syndrome, cisplatin, or vitamin B6 toxicity
Guillain-Barre spectrum and chronic inflammatory neuropathies
Vitamin B12 deficiency with subacute combined degeneration
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-Hu (ANNA-1) and broader paraneoplastic antibody panel
CT chest and FDG-PET to detect occult small-cell lung cancer, with bronchoscopy or biopsy as needed
MRI brain and spine, which may show medial temporal or brainstem signal change
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for pleocytosis and oligoclonal bands
Nerve conduction studies confirming a sensory neuronopathy
Electroencephalography where encephalitis or seizures are suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalitis with seizures or reduced consciousness
Brainstem or bulbar involvement threatening airway and swallow
Severe autonomic failure with cardiovascular or gastrointestinal instability
Positive anti-Hu antibodies indicating a very high probability of underlying malignancy
Respiratory compromise from neuromuscular or central involvement
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with neurological deficits often stabilising rather than reversing after treatment; overall outcome is strongly determined by the underlying small-cell lung cancer, though treating the tumour may slow neurological progression.
pitfalls: Overlooking an occult small-cell lung cancer when initial imaging is negative
Misdiagnosing the sensory neuronopathy as a peripheral neuropathy of other cause
Expecting substantial neurological recovery from immunotherapy alone
Failing to recognise the multifocal nature and attributing each deficit separately
Delaying tumour treatment, which offers the best chance of stabilisation
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Intensive search for and treatment of the underlying small-cell lung cancer, offering the best chance of halting neurological progression
Immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, recognising that response is often limited owing to T-cell-mediated neuronal loss
Antiseizure medication for seizures and symptomatic treatment of the painful sensory neuronopathy with neuropathic-pain agents
Supportive management of autonomic failure, including orthostatic hypotension and gastrointestinal dysmotility
Rehabilitation for sensory ataxia and multidisciplinary supportive and palliative care
Neurology-oncology follow-up with ongoing tumour surveillance where the cancer is initially occult
